Ainsi, en n'agissant pas conformément au principe de précaution qui exige de prendre toutes les mesures nécessaires pour assurer la protection de la victime, mais également de celle de sa famille, l'État s'est rendu complice sinon responsable des actes de restrictions de la liberté de M. Audace Vianney et de sa femme ainsi que des atteintes à l'intégrité physique de la victime ayant résulté à sa mort. Par conséquent, la Commission constate que l'État violé les principes de l'article 6 du fait de son inaction.

L'article 7(1) (a) de la Charte africaine dispose que « toute personne a droit à ce que sa cause soit entendue. Ce droit comprend, le droit de saisir les juridictions nationales compétentes de tout acte violant les droits fondamentaux qui lui sont reconnus et garantis par les conventions, les lois, règlements et coutumes en vigueur (...) »

L'article 26 quant à lui fait obligation aux États de « garantir l'indépendance des Tribunaux et de permettre l'établissement et le perfectionnement d'institutions nationales appropriées chargées de la promotion et de la protection des droits et libertés garantis par la Charte. »

Les Plaintants soumettent que la Commission a déjà eu l'occasion de constater une violation des articles 7(1) (a) et 26 de la Charte africaine dans des situations où l'impartialité des tribunaux n'est pas garantie notamment en raison de la nomination des juges par les autorités gouvernementales et politiques.

Par ailleurs l'analyse de sa jurisprudence fournit des exemples d'obstacles pouvant empêcher l'accès des victimes aux tribunaux et/ou la partialité des tribunaux. Nonobstant cet état de fait, il revient à la Commission d'établir à lumière des faits et arguments qui lui sont soumis si dans le cas d'espèce la même conclusion peut s'appliquer.
La Commission va dans un premier temps procéder à l'analyse des faits pour déterminer s'il y a eu violation de l'article 7 (1) (a) et ensuite se pencher sur la violation alléguée de l'article 26.

Concernant la violation de l'article 7(1) (a) il est soumis que suite à la tentative d'assassinat sur la personne de M. Audace Vianney en mars 2011, un dossier judiciaire avait été ouvert par le Ministère public.

Le droit de voir sa cause entendue suppose que les mesures nécessaires à la résolution du préjudice subi soient concrètement mises en œuvre en vue de rétablir la victime dans son droit. Dans le cas d'espèce, hormis l'ouverture d'un dossier par le Ministère public suite à la tentative d'assassinat de M. Audace Vianney en 2011, aucune autre action n'a été menée. D'ailleurs, les résultats de l'enquête que l'Etat dit avoir ouverte n'ont jamais été communiqués aux Plaintants faisant ainsi douter de son existence. Pour justifier la lenteur de la procédure, sinon l'inaction, l'Etat défendeur avance l'argument du refus des parents de la victime de répondre aux convocations qui leurs auraient été adressées dans le cadre de l'instruction de cette affaire, mais il n'apporte aucune preuve de l'existence desdites convocations que la famille dit n'avoir jamais reçues.

Ensuite, sur la base de la jurisprudence établie par le Comité contre la torture des Nations Unies, l'Etat a l'obligation d'enquêter dans des cas de graves violations des droits de l'homme telle que la torture. Par ailleurs, dans son observation générale sur le droit à la vie, la Commission recommande aux États d'adopter des mesures aussi bien pour prévenir les privations arbitraires de la vie que de mener des enquêtes rapides, impartiales, approfondies et transparentes sur toute privation de ce type ayant pu se produire, en amenant les responsables à répondre de leurs actes (...). De ce fait une violation avérée du droit à la vie, devrait pouvoir faire l'objet de la même obligation et partant la diligence de la justice prévaloir. Cette diligence pourrait se traduire par une protection adéquate donnée à la victime et la célérité de l'enquête sur la tentative d'assassinat, mais surtout dans la recherche des responsables de son exécution extrajudiciaire pour laquelle aucune poursuite n'a été entamée.

Dans l'affaire Association of Victims of Post Electoral Violence et Interights c. Cameroun, la Commission met un accent particulier sur l'obligation de l'Etat de « mener des investigations » et de « prendre des mesures conséquentes » pour empêcher la violation mais également y remédier. L'obligation d'enquêter et de poursuivre est réitérée dans Sudan Human Rights Organisation et Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) c. Soudan, où la Commission a conclu que l'absence d'enquête dans les cas d'exécutions arbitraires et extrajudiciaires équivaut à une violation du droit à la vie.

En l'espèce, les Plaintants ont soumis que si le dossier judiciaire ouvert relativement à la tentative d'assassinat de mars 2011 a abouti à l'inculpation de M Cyrille Nahimana, ce dernier n'a jamais été arrêté. Il apparaît donc que les voies de recours internes ont été activées mais le résultat s'est avéré inefficace et insatisfaisant pour ce premier incident. Ensuite concernant son exécution extrajudiciaire, aucun dossier judiciaire n'a été ouvert et les personnes responsables de son exécution n'ont pas été identifiées selon les déclarations du Procureur général. Les Plaintants estiment donc que la famille a été empêchée d'accéder à un tribunal dans la pratique.
Suite à l'analyse des arguments des Plaintants à l'aune de la jurisprudence établie, la Commission conclut à une violation des dispositions de l'article 7(1) (a) de la Charte

Concernant la violation alléguée de l'article 26, relatif à l'exigence d'indépendance des tribunaux il convient de l'analyser en combinaison avec l'article 7(1) (d), qui se rapporte au principe d'impartialité prévue à l'article 7 1(d) de la Charte africaine, même si ce dernier n'a guère été évoqué par les Plaintants, la Commission estime qu'il est nécessaire de l'associer à l'analyse présente. Ainsi, si parfois on désigne la nécessaire impartialité du juge sous le vocable « indépendance », L'impartialité se rapproche beaucoup plus de l'indépendance personnelle du magistrat par opposition à l'indépendance collective de la magistrature. L'indépendance se ramène à un « statut » et l'impartialité à un « état d'esprit ».

Dans ses Directives et principes sur le droit à un procès équitable et à l'assistance judiciaire en Afrique, la Commission va dans le même sens en indiquant que la garantie d'un procès équitable suppose l'existence d'une instance juridictionnelle indépendante et impartiale.Ceci suppose que l'indépendance des instances juridictionnelles et celles des juges doit être garantie par la constitution et les lois du pays et créée par la loi pour rendre des décisions au sujet de questions respectées de tous ; gouvernement, institutions et autorités. Par ailleurs, les magistrats se doivent de régler les affaires dont ils sont saisis sans restrictions et sans être l'objet d'influences, incitations, pressions, menaces ou interventions indues, directes ou indirectes, de la part de qui que ce soit ou pour quelque raison que ce soit, pour en garantir son impartialité.

En l'espèce, les Plaignants font valoir que des nombreux cas de violations flagrantes des droits de l'homme impliquant des agents de l'Etat y compris des actes de tortures ou des atteintes à la vie, ne font pas l'objet d'un suivi rigoureux de la part de la justice et dans les rares cas ayant abouti, les peines ou les dédommagement des victimes sont insignifiants au vu des préjudices subis.Ils ont également évoqué l'absence d'indépendance du système judiciaire vis-à-vis du pouvoir exécutif, ce qui représente un obstacle majeur à la lutte contre l'impunité.

Si dans sa décision Organisation Mondiale Contre la Torture et Ligue de la Zone Afrique pour la Défense des Droits des Enfants et Elèves (pour le compte de Céline) c. République Démocratique du Congo, la Commission avait estimé que le seul défaut d'efficacité des procédures concernées ne peuvent suffire à établir le manque d'indépendance des tribunaux qui suppose nécessairement des éléments d'interférence extérieure, particulièrement en l'absence de preuves soutenant cette allégation, dans le cas présent, les conclusions des Etats généraux de la justice burundaise tenues du 5 au 9 aout 2013 ont mis en exergue, la nécessité de réformer le système pour en assurer son indépendance, notamment vis-à-vis de l'exécutif, sujet de préoccupation central durant les discussions.

S'agissant de l'impunité généralisée au Burundi notamment sur les questions d'exécutions extrajudiciaire, la Commission d'enquête des Nations Unies sur le Burundi à dans son rapport de 2017 a relevé de longs délais dans les procédures judiciaires, l'organisation de certains procès sensibles dans l'enceinte de prisons, avec un effet dissuasif sur la présence d'observateurs, ainsi que des procès expéditifs en application de la procédure de « flagrance ». Elle a également souligné le manque d'indépendance du système judiciaire observé de longue date au Burundi a aggravé l'impunité régnant dans le pays. Par ailleurs, des multiples rapports produits par diverses organisations internationales ont également constaté l'impunité rampantes dans

des violences faites aux filles et particulièrement le viol en RDC, avait conduit la Commission à conclure que le cas de la victime n'était pas isolé. Les cas d'impunité au Burundi, particulièrement en ce qui concerne les exécutions extrajudiciaires ont été rapportées par plusieurs organisations internationales y compris les Nations Unies. Sur cette base l'indépendance de la justice peut donc être questionnée. La Commission est donc d'avis qu'il y a violation de l'article 26 de la Charte.

Les Plaintants soumettent que les droits de la famille de M. Audace Vianney ont été violés, du fait de son exécution extrajudiciaire mais également des faits de tortures, actes d'intimidations et de harcèlements dont il a fait l'objet.

L'article 18(1) de la Charte africaine consacre la famille comme étant l'élément naturel et la base de la société et par conséquent elle doit être protégée par l'Etat qui veille à sa santé physique et morale.

La Commission a clairement énoncé que la séparation des membres d'une famille constitue une violation au droit contenu à l'article 18(1), elle a également rappelé que l'Etat a une obligation positive à l'égard de la famille, qu'il se doit d'assister dans la ses propres agents et organes et par des parties tierces.

La Déclaration des principes fondamentaux de justice relatifs aux victimes de la criminalité et aux victimes d'abus de pouvoir, adoptée par l'Assemblée générale dans sa résolution 40/34 du 29 novembre 1985, considère comme "victimes" des personnes qui, individuellement ou collectivement, ont subi un préjudice, notamment une atteinte à leur intégrité physique ou mentale, une souffrance morale, une perte matérielle, ou une atteinte grave à leurs droits fondamentaux, en raison d'actes ou d'omissions qui enfreignent les lois pénales en vigueur dans un Etat Membre. Il peut s'agir de la famille proche ou des personnes à la charge de la victime directe.

Au-delà des dispositions contenues dans la Charte africaine il est unanimement accepté que la famille constitue le socle de la société, particulièrement en Afrique où elle revêt un caractère sacré. Ainsi, assurer la protection de la famille c'est préserver l'équilibre de la nation. Il est donc primordial de s'assurer que cette protection se fasse selon les normes établies.

Dans le cas d'espèce, la famille de M. Audace Vianney a souffert des actes de torture, traitement inhumains et dégradants, des intimidations et du harcèlement subi par la victime qui l'ont également affectée. Ensuite, elle a subie l'angoisse et la détresse émotionnelle causée par son décès. A cela s'ajoute les inquiétudes pour sa sécurité physique mais aussi économique avec la mort de la victime qui subvenait aux besoins de sa famille. Enfin, son enfant s'est retrouvé orphelin à un très jeune âge, le privant de l'un de ses parents. Ceci peut constituer une violation de l'article 18(3) de la Charte africaine des droits et du bien-être de l'enfant africain, qui dispose qu'aucun enfant ne peut être privé de son entretien en raison du statut marital de ses parents. La mère de cet enfant étant devenue veuve suite au décès de son père, l'entretien de ce dernier est désormais incertain avec la perte de celui qui assurait la sécurité financière ce qui rend son avenir aléatoire.

Il convient maintenant d'analyser si l'Etat a failli ou non à son obligation positive envers la famille il pèse également une obligation négative qui est celle d'empêcher la violation des droits et des intérêts de la famille. La sécurité, physique et morale de la famille implique la protection des droits sociaux économiques qui permettent sa réalisation. Dans leurs soumissions, les Plaintants ont clairement indiqué que la victime n'avait bénéficié d'aucune protection malgré la tentative d'assassinat dont elle avait été victime. Fait aggravant, cette tentative d'assassinat avait été commise par les agents de l'Etat de même que les multiples actes de tortures et autres actes d'intimidations et de harcèlement à son endroit.

Au vu de ce qui précède il ne fait aucun doute que l'Etat n'a pas été capable de protéger la victime dont la mort a occasionnée une perte irrémissible pour sa famille. Particulièrement en tenant compte du fait qu'il avait été dûment informé de la situation de la victime. La Commission constate donc la violation effective de l'article 18(1) par l'Etat défendeur.

L'article 1 de la Charte africaine impose aux États parties à la Charte africaine de reconnaître les droits qui y sont garantis et d'adopter des mesures législatives et autres pour donner effet à ces droits, devoirs et libertés.

La jurisprudence de la Commission a établi que toute violation de l'une des dispositions de la Charte africaine, entraîne automatiquement la violation de l'article 1 En d'autres termes, si un État partie n'assure pas le respect des droits contenus dans la Charte africaine, cela constitue une violation de la Charte africaine.

À cet égard, et après avoir constaté que l'État défendeur a violé plusieurs articles de la Charte africaine, à savoir les articles 2, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) (a) et 26 et 18(1), la Commission conclut que l'État défendeur a violé l'article 1 de la Charte africaine.

En outre, cette responsabilité est automatiquement engagée dès qu'il est conclu à la violation d'un droit protégé par la Charte. Au vu de tout ce qui précède, la Commission conclut à une violation des dispositions de l'article 1. La Commission,Par ces motifs,
Dit que la République du Burundi a violé les dispositions des articles 2, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) (a) lu conjointement avec 26 et 18(1) de la Charte.

En conséquence : i. Demande à la République du Burundi de mener une enquête approfondie sur l'exécution de la victime et les autres violations subies par des organes judiciaires indépendantes; ii. De mettre en place des mécanismes pour lutter contre l'impunité généralisée en matière d'exécution extrajudiciaire et d'atteintes au droit à la vie ; iii. Demande en outre à la République du Burundi d'accorder aux ayants droits de la Victime une réparation adéquate et suffisante ainsi que l'assistance médicale et psychologique nécessaire, s'il y a toujours lieu ; iv. S'assurer de la pleine application de la Loi n° 1/04 du 27 juin 2016 portant protection des victimes, des témoins et d'autres personnes en situation de risque ; v. Demande à la République du Burundi d'adopter toutes les mesures nécessaires pour que de tels faits ne se reproduisent pas et s'assurer la loi sur les partis politiques respectent les principes démocratiques et le pluralisme politique ; vi. Mettre en œuvre les recommandations du rapport de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples sur sa mission d'établissement des faits au Burundi tenue du 7 au 13 décembre 2015 vii. Demande enfin à la République du Burundi de lui rapporter par écrit, dans les cent quatre-vingt jours (180) jours de la notification de la présente décision, quant aux mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de ces recommandations. Adoptée lors de la 68 Session ordinaire de la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples tenue virtuellement du 14 avril au 4 mai 2021

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received on 9 June 2014, a Communication submitted pursuant to Article 55 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) by the Action by Christians for the Abolition of Torture (ACAT-Burundi), the Association for the Protection of Human Rights and Detained Persons (APRODH), the Forum for the Strengthening of Civil Society (FORSC), the Forum for Conscience and Development (FOCODE) and TrackImpunityAlways (TRIAL) hereinafter referred to as "the Complainants" on behalf of the late Audace Vianney Habonarugira hereinafter referred to as "Audace Vianney" or the "First victim" and his family hereinafter referred to as the "Second victim" or the "family of the First victim".
The Communication was submitted against the Republic of Burundi (hereinafter referred to as the Respondent State or Burundi), a State that ratified the African Charter on 28 July 1989.

The Complainants report that the First victim, born in 1983, was a married Burundian citizen and father of one child. They state that he was a colonel in the National Liberation Forces (FNL) and that after his demobilisation, he had retrained as a driver and mechanic.

The Complainants explain that the FNL was a rebel movement that laid down its arms in 2009 and constituted itself as a political party. They also indicate that after presidential and parliamentary elections largely boycotted by the opposition, FNL members began to suffer from 2010 a policy of repression, extrajudicial executions and other types of attacks.

The Complainants report that even after his demobilisation, the First victim had kept in contact with the FNL authorities and that from January 2011, he began to receive serious threats from the police and the intelligence services. They state that Mr Cyrille Nahimana, an agent of the National Intelligence Service (SNR) repeatedly and unsuccessfully asked Audace Vianney to collaborate with him by providing the names of certain FNL members.

The Complainants report that on 07 March 2011, as the First victim was about to leave his home, Mr Cyrille Nahimana and other individuals arrived and took him a few metres from his house and shot him in the leg, the hip and the stomach. The Complainants inform that the First victim fell into a coma and that on the day of the attempted homicide, his wife was arrested and detained with her child who, at the time, was two years old.

The Complainants report that after about 3 and a half months of convalescence, the First victim was able to leave the hospital on 27 June 2011 and began to live in hiding because he was still being sought despite what he had been through.

The Complainants report that on 14 July 2011, Aurace Vianney who had an appointment with one of his friends Mr Claude Kwizera called his wife to inform her that the appointment had in fact been made by an impostor; they add that the telephone call to his wife was suddenly interrupted and that his family was no longer able to reach him by telephone. They report that on 15 July 2011, the bodies of the First victim and of his friend Mr Claude Kwizera were found on a hill in the commune of Isare and that the bodies bore gunshot wounds.

The Complainants report that a judicial file relating to the first attempted homicide of March 2011 had been opened and that in this regard Mr Cyrille Nahimana was charged but was not arrested. They indicate that the report of 14 August 2012 of the Commission of Inquiry set up by the Prosecutor General of the Republic "to shed light on the cases that some reports describe as extrajudicial executions or torture" states that a file and an investigation were opened following the execution of the First victim but that the case is still under investigation. The Complainants allege that no effective and impartial investigation has in fact been conducted by the Respondent State.

The Complainants maintain that the relentless persecution of the First victim and his execution plunged the Second victim into great terror, making the use of local remedies dangerous for them. They report that a friend of the First victim who had helped the family search for him during his disappearance on 14 July 2011, had been arbitrarily imprisoned. They emphasise that the detention of the wife of the First victim and her child in March 2011, combined with the threats that the family of the First victim had received during her detention further heighten their fears for their very lives. They further maintain that the climate of impunity prevailing in Burundi makes this fear entirely legitimate.

The Complainants further indicate that there is no legal and institutional framework in Burundi for the protection of victims and witnesses of human rights violations, that the Respondent State should be required to adopt provisional measures to avoid reprisals against the Second victim and the witnesses during the period of examination of the case by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission).

The Complainants furthermore allege that the case of the First victim is not isolated, that there are in Burundi several cases of serious violations, notably extrajudicial executions, arbitrary detentions and torture. They base their allegations mainly on reports of the United Nations Office in Burundi and other organisations dating from 2010, 2011 and 2012 and on recommendations made to Burundi during the universal periodic review in 2013. They maintain that the majority of the cases have remained unpunished.
The Complainants affirm that the matter has not been submitted to another international body for the settlement of disputes or of similar competence.
The Complainants allege the violation of the following articles of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter): 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 (1) (a), 18 (1) and 26.

The Complainants request the Commission to: a. Grant provisional measures to the family of the First victim and to the witnesses; b. Consider the referral of the Communication to the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Court) pursuant to Rule 118.3 of the Rules of Procedure of the Commission; c. Declare the Communication admissible; d. Find that the facts reveal a violation by the Respondent State of the following articles of the African Charter: 2, 4, 5, 6 read together with Article 1 with respect to the First victim and 5, 7 (1) (a), 18 (1) and 26 read together with Article 1 with respect to the Second victim; e. Order Burundi, in application of Articles 7 (1) (a) and 26 of the African Charter, to conduct a prompt, thorough and effective investigation into the execution of the victim and the other violations suffered, by independent and impartial judicial bodies with a view to prosecuting and punishing the perpetrators. Require Burundi to immediately suspend administratively the alleged perpetrators pending the institution of proceedings; f. Order Burundi to provide appropriate reparation to the rightful claimants of the victim. Require Burundi to give guarantees of non-repetition, in particular through public apologies addressed to the relatives of the victim and a strong message condemning such acts and their impunity; g. Request Burundi to adopt as a matter of urgency, legislation aimed at protecting victims and witnesses, notably in the case of judicial proceedings, in order to effectively guarantee the right of access to the courts; h. Request Burundi to adopt all necessary measures so that such facts do not recur and to ensure political pluralism; i. Request Burundi to publish the findings of the Commission; j. Order Burundi to report, within a period of 3 months, on the follow-up it has given to the conclusions of the Commission.
The Complaint reached the Secretariat of the African Commission on 09 June 2014. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 13 June 2014.

At its 16th Extraordinary Session held in Kigali from 20 to 29 July 2014 in Rwanda, the African Commission considered the Communication and decided to be seized of it. The Commission also requested the taking of provisional measures by the Respondent State but rejected the request for referral of the matter to the Court.

By letter dated 12 August 2014, the Secretariat informed the Complainants and the Respondent State of the seizure of the Communication and at the same time, sent a copy of the Communication to the Respondent State and invited the Complainants to submit their arguments on admissibility within two (02) months from notification.
On 16 October 2014, the Complainants transmitted a correspondence to the Secretariat, inviting the Commission to refer to their arguments on admissibility contained in their initial submissions.

On 28 October 2014, the Secretariat sent back to the Respondent State, copies of the Complainants' initial submissions and invited it to refer to the Complainants' arguments on admissibility and to transmit its own within two (02) months from notification.

On 24 March 2015, the Respondent State received a letter from the Secretariat informing it that at its 17th Extraordinary Session held in Banjul, The Gambia, from 19 to 28 February 2015, the African Commission noted that the two (02) month period had not been complied with and decided to grant it an additional period of 30 calendar days from notification to transmit its observations on admissibility.

On 18 May 2015, the African Commission sent the Respondent State two notes verbales, informing it respectively that at its 56th Ordinary Session, the Commission noted that the extension previously granted had not been complied with, and then decided to defer its decision on the admissibility of the Communication in view of time constraints.

On 1 June 2015, the Secretariat received a report from Burundi on the implementation of the provisional measures taken to protect the victims; the Secretariat transmitted it to the complainants on 04 June 2015.

On 22 June 2015, the Secretariat received the observations of Burundi on the admissibility of the Communication and transmitted them to the Complainants by letter of 24 June 2015 and the latter responded to them on 08 July 2015.

On 13 August 2015, the Secretariat informed the parties that the Commission had decided at its 18th Extraordinary Session held from 29 July to 07 August 2015, to defer its decision on the admissibility of the Communication to its 57th Ordinary Session in order to take into account all the documents transmitted by the parties on admissibility.

During its 24th Extraordinary Session held from 30 July to 8 August 2018, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declared the communication admissible and informed the parties in accordance with the provisions of Rule 108 of its Rules of Procedure.

The Complainants maintain that the Communication should be declared admissible. In their argumentation, the Complainants dwelt rather on the requirement set out in Article 56 (5) of the African Charter.

The Complainants maintain that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies should not stand in the way of the admissibility of the present Communication. The Complainants invoke 3 grounds in support of this position; they maintain indeed that local remedies have been unduly prolonged, that they have proved ineffective and unsatisfactory and that it is dangerous to use them.

First, the Complainants consider that the remedies have been unduly prolonged. One of the positions maintained by the Complainants throughout their arguments on admissibility is that acts of torture and violations of the right to life constitute serious human rights violations and that consequently the State must automatically initiate an investigation but that even having been informed on several occasions of the case of Audace Vianney, the Burundian authorities remained passive and lack the will to establish responsibility in this matter. They indicate that in the present case, the facts date from 14 July 2011 and that two years and nine (2 years and 9 months) months later, they remain unpunished; that this state of affairs shows a "notorious lack of will" on the part of the Respondent State because according to them, in other cases sometimes even more complex, particular speed has marked the investigation and the trial.

Second, the Complainants maintain that local remedies have proved ineffective and unsatisfactory. In support of this allegation, the Complainants affirm on the one hand that no member of the family of the First victim was ever heard or called in connection with the investigation of the case, that the existence of an autopsy report has not been established and that the results of the investigation, if there has been an investigation, were never communicated either to the family or to the Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) that followed up this case. The Complainants further affirm that the general climate of impunity crowned by the lack of independence of magistrates as well as the lack of qualified personnel also contribute to demonstrating the ineffective and unsatisfactory nature of local remedies.

Finally, the Complainants maintain that it is dangerous to use local remedies. They insist indeed on the fact that the harassment suffered by the first victim and his family, plunged the latter into acute terror. The Complainants recall that the wife of Audace Vianney, Mrs Noella Niyonkuru, had according to them, been arbitrarily arrested and detained with her child following the attempted assassination of the First victim on 7 March 2011. They add that the present case is not isolated and that the high number of extrajudicial executions committed by agents of the National Police and the Intelligence Services reinforces the fears of the Second victim since according to them, it is these same actors who are singled out in the present case. They maintain that in similar cases, relatives of victims have been subjected to infringements of their liberty and have been threatened as soon as they sought to obtain justice, that the members of the family of the first victim fear for their lives all the more as they come from a modest background, making their situation precarious from the financial, psychological and security standpoint. The Complainants add that there do not exist in Burundi, measures aimed at protecting Complainants and witnesses against any ill-treatment following the lodging of a complaint or the giving of a statement; that this reinforces the vulnerability of the Second victim especially as according to them, the persons alleged to be responsible for the facts are members of the National Police and the Intelligence Services enjoying significant powers and means of pressure...

The Respondent State maintains that the Communication should be declared inadmissible for failure to comply with the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies required by Article 56 (5) of the Charter.

The Respondent State justifies its position by maintaining that the facts of which the Commission is seized still fall within the jurisdiction of the Burundian courts because the Public Prosecutor's Office has opened a criminal file under number RMP 137 164/NR/BB. It informs that the magistrates of the public prosecutor's office are at work conducting an investigation which must aim at seeking serious indications of guilt of the perpetrator of the offence without disregarding the guarantees necessary for the exercise of the right to defence (articles 3, 10 and 72 of Law No. 1/10 of 03 April 2013 revising the Code of Criminal Procedure of Burundi), which involves investigation for and against the accused (article 72 of the same law) in respect of the presumption of innocence. The Respondent State therefore maintains that the Complainants were hasty in seizing the Commission, local remedies according to it not yet being exhausted given that the file has not been closed by the competent Prosecutor's Office.

In their additional observations, the Complainants indicated that the Respondent State's submissions on admissibility do not bring a new substantial element, that there is reason to doubt its statements. The Complainants refer the Commission to their initial submissions and specify that the arguments on admissibility contained therein remain fully valid and no new element is to be brought to the attention of the Commission.
Article 56 of the African Charter prescribes seven (7) conditions which must be cumulatively fulfilled for a Communication to be declared admissible by the Commission.

In the present case, only one of the conditions, namely that provided for in Article 56 (5) of the Charter is contested by the parties. After thorough examination of the file, the Commission is itself satisfied that the six (6) other conditions provided for in Articles 56 (1), (2), (3), (4), (6) and (7) are fulfilled.

Indeed, the authors of the Communication have indicated their identity; the Communication concerns alleged violations of the African Charter said to have been committed in 2011, that is to say well after the entry into force of the African Charter in Burundi. The Communication does not contain disparaging or insulting language towards the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union; the information communicated by the Complainants in the Communication derives, among other things, from testimonies and reports of human rights organisations. Moreover, it does not emerge from the file that the present case has already been settled in accordance with either the principles of the United Nations Charter, or the Charter of the Organisation of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter. As regards the requirement set out in Article 56 (6), in its Communication Tsatsu Tsikata v. Republic of Ghana, the Commission has already noted the link between Article 56 (5) and Article 56 (6), it therefore intends to rule on Article 56 (6) after the analysis of Article 56 (5).

As to Article 56 (5) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights which is contested by the parties, it provides that to be admissible, the Communication must "be sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged".

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has also developed exceptions to the rule of exhaustion of local remedies. In its decision on the Communication Sir Dawda K. Jawara v. The Gambia, the Commission indeed indicated that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies cannot apply if the remedies in question are not available, effective or satisfactory. The Commission has also established the fact that if the complainant cannot go before a court in his or her country because he or she fears for his or her life or for that of members of his or her family, the remedies are considered non-existent for him or her.

To recall, the Complainants maintain that with regard to this Communication, the Commission must exempt them from the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies because according to them, the local remedies procedure has been unduly prolonged, the remedies have proved ineffective and unsatisfactory and it is dangerous to use them.

On the first ground of the Complainants, namely that the remedies have been unduly prolonged, they consider that two years and nine months (2 years and 9) months after the occurrence of the facts, they remain unpunished; that no effective, diligent and prompt investigation has been conducted into the facts despite their gravity.

Before any examination of the normal or abnormal nature of the prolongation of the local remedies procedure, the Commission considers it necessary to rule on the absence of a formal Complaint by the Complainants to the national judicial authorities. The Complainants maintain indeed that in the event of allegations of serious violations such as torture, the State must automatically initiate an investigation even in the absence of a complaint in due form. The Commission has already indicated in its jurisprudence, that even if the victims of criminal acts have not brought legal action, the State as guarantor of public order must initiate an investigation. In any event, the Respondent State has not challenged the absence of a formal Complaint, it indicated that the file is at the investigation stage. It is therefore the normal or abnormal nature of the prolongation of this remedy set in motion by the Respondent State by virtue of its obligation to investigate that must be assessed.

Not only must the State initiate an investigation and prosecution when there are reasonable grounds to believe that a criminal act has been committed but this must also be done promptly in accordance with the relevant international instruments, notably in the event of allegations of serious crimes such as torture. Indeed, the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment to which Burundi acceded on 18 February 1993 provides in its Article 12 that "Each State Party shall ensure that its competent authorities proceed to a prompt and impartial investigation, wherever there is reasonable ground to believe that an act of torture has been committed in any territory under its jurisdiction". The Guidelines and Measures for the Prohibition and Prevention of Torture, Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (Robben Island Guidelines) adopted by the Commission to complement Article 5 of the African Charter provide that "In the case of allegations of torture or ill-treatment, an impartial and effective investigation should be initiated without delay..."

The promptness of the procedure for establishing responsibility, beginning with the investigation, is undoubtedly a key factor. The Commission notes that two years and nine months or even 4 years (at the time of the transmission of the Respondent State's arguments) is a long period for an investigation which is still not completed especially in view of the gravity of the alleged facts. However, it is not so much the prolongation in itself that is in question, but it is the normal or abnormal nature of the prolongation of the remedies set in motion that must be examined. In this respect, the Commission has already emphasised notably in its decision Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Zimbabwe, the need to take into consideration the circumstances of the case and the reasons advanced to justify the prolongation of the remedies in order to determine whether the prolongation is normal or abnormal. The Court noted this principle by indicating that "the assessment of the normal or abnormal nature of the procedure relating to local remedies must be made on a case-by-case basis, according to the circumstances specific to each case". The Commission will therefore examine in the light of the applicable legal instruments, the facts and the circumstances of the case whether the remedies in question have been prolonged in a normal or abnormal manner.

In the present case, the Respondent State maintains that the Complainants were hasty in seizing the Commission because the file is at the investigation stage which is conducted for and against the accused in respect of the presumption of innocence in accordance with articles 3, 10 and 72 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Commission also notes that the Respondent State's report on the implementation of provisional measures contains certain statements relevant to the admissibility of the Communication which should be considered in the examination of the admissibility of the Communication in the interest of the proper administration of justice even if these statements do not appear in its submissions on admissibility. Indeed, the Respondent State maintained in the said report, that the witnesses and the members of the victim's family no longer appear despite the multiple summonses sent to them to enlighten the judges. The Respondent State maintains that the Complainants and victims are protected like other citizens and that if they were threatened, they would already have lodged a complaint. It must be deduced that it emerges from the Respondent State's submissions that the prolongation of the procedure is linked to the need to satisfy respect for the presumption of innocence and to the failure of the witnesses and members of the family of Audace Vianney to appear in response to summonses.

Even though the Commission is of the view that the investigation must be conducted for and against the accused, it is of the view, with the Court, that respect for the presumption of innocence, which is a legitimate concern, should not exempt the Respondent State from moving the proceedings initiated forward reasonably.

The Commission notes that the Respondent State did not respond to the Complainants' allegation that in certain more complex cases, the Respondent State conducted prosecution and trial with speed. The Respondent State merely indicated that the investigation is conducted for and against the accused without indicating in detail why the investigation for and against the accused needs to run for 2 years and 9 months in the present case and even almost four years since it emerges from the Respondent State's submissions received on 22 June 2015, that the file is still at the investigation stage.

As indicated above, the Respondent State maintained in its report on the implementation of provisional measures, that the witnesses and the members of the victim's family no longer appear despite the multiple summonses sent to them to enlighten the judges. This assertion which seems to justify the slowness of the procedure deserves some attention. The Complainants in their submissions, indicated that no member of the family was ever heard or called in connection with the investigation of the file. The Commission is of the view, with the Court, that regarding the identification of perpetrators of crimes, it is precisely the responsibility of the Respondent State to implement all the means at its disposal to find the alleged perpetrators even when they are initially unknown. The Commission notes in this regard, that the Respondent State has not placed on the record, material proof of the summonses issued. In any event, the Commission notes the fact that the Public Prosecutor's Office, by way of the prerogatives linked to the exercise of public action must in principle have the necessary means to cause to appear any person whose hearing is necessary in the examination of a file. Along the same lines, the Commission notes that Law No. 1/10 of 03 April 2013 revising the Code of Criminal Procedure cited by the Respondent State itself, indicates in its articles 79, 82, 83, 335 and 336, a list of diligent actions (warrant to bring, referral before the competent judge, summons to appear) that the Public Prosecutor's Office can implement to bring the persons summoned to appear. The Respondent State has however not indicated what diligent actions were implemented in accordance with its obligations, to hear the witnesses and the Second victim in this case.

Furthermore, it is rather surprising that the members of the family of the First victim and the witnesses do not wish to respond to the summonses. If it turned out that they are afraid, it would still be incumbent on the Respondent State, in accordance with its international obligations especially in the event of allegations of torture, to take the necessary measures to ensure that victims and witnesses feel safe enough to respond favourably to summonses. Indeed, Article 13 of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment to which Burundi is a party provides that the Respondent State must take the necessary steps to "ensure that the complainant and witnesses are protected against all ill-treatment or intimidation as a consequence of his complaint or any evidence given". The Guidelines and Measures for the Prohibition and Prevention of Torture, Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment provide that "States should take measures to protect from violence, threats of violence or any other form of intimidation or reprisal, victims of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, witnesses, those investigating, human rights defenders and their families, as a result of complaints lodged, hearings held, statements made, reports made or investigations conducted".

In view of the nature of the alleged violations, which requires a prompt investigation in order to establish responsibility and in the face of the absence of sufficient justification by the Respondent State to explain why since the discovery of the death of Audace Vianney on 15 July 2011, the file is still at the investigation stage and in view particularly of the lack of elements showing all the diligence the State displayed to cause the witnesses and members of the family of the First victim to appear, the Commission considers that the delays in the present case have been unduly prolonged.

As regards Article 56 (6) of the African Charter which prescribes that the Communication must "be submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized with the matter", it should be emphasised again that in the present case, the parties agree on the fact that local remedies have not been exhausted. Having already established the fact that the remedies are unduly prolonged and not being able to identify in the Respondent State's code of criminal procedure the time limit for the investigation of such a file (all the more so as the State does not indicate exactly at what stage of the investigation the file is), it is for the Commission to count the time of its seizure from the moment when the Complainants should reasonably have become aware of the undue prolongation of local remedies.

From the Complainants' submissions, it appears to the Commission that it is 2 years and 9 months after the facts that the Complainants were convinced of the undue prolongation of local remedies thus on 15 April 2014 that is almost two (2) months before the seizure of the Commission on 09 June 2014. The Commission notes however that the Complainants' submissions contain material elements which show that they should have realised it earlier. Indeed, the Complainants indicated that in a report of 14 August 2012, the Respondent State indicated that the file of Audace Vianney was under investigation, a fact not contested by the Respondent State. This report would constitute a first indication of the length of time taken to investigate the file. Moreover, the Complainants should have had firmer indications as to the undue prolongation of the remedies. In addition, the questioning of the members of the family would have allowed them to corroborate the hypothesis that the remedies have been prolonged as the last statement placed on the record dates from 11 December 2013. The Complainants seized the Commission on 09 June 2014 that is almost six (6) months after having had sufficient knowledge of the state of progress of the file and of the means of supporting the allegations of violations and more particularly the thesis of the undue prolongation of local remedies.

Furthermore, the time observed by the Complainants before seizing the Commission does not prejudice the capacity of the Commission to analyse the facts set out before it. In view of the alleged violations requiring a reaction from the Respondent State, the complainants deemed it appropriate to be sufficiently convinced of the undue prolongation of the remedies, then to incorporate into the Communication the appreciable and sustainable elements to strengthen such a finding (undue prolongation), if it is true that the Commission in a jurisprudential precedent has established the close link between reasonable time and undue prolongation of remedies, the six-month period between the seizure and the last statement placed on the record as a supporting element could not be characterised as unreasonable.
Thus, in the Commission's understanding, the time within which it was seized is reasonable it being understood also that some time is needed to gather all the documents of the file.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the present Communication admissible in accordance with the provisions of Article 56 of the African Charter.

Following the Commission's decision to declare the communication in question admissible, the parties were informed of the decision and invited to present their arguments on the merits of the Communication, in accordance with the provisions of Rule 108 of the Rules of Procedure.

Following the Secretariat's request asking them to submit their arguments on the Merits, the Complainants requested that the Secretariat refer to their initial submissions. The latter were therefore transmitted to the Respondent State so that it could also submit its statement of defence.

By Note Verbale No. 204.02.01/1495/MAE/2018/BMF, the State contested the decision on admissibility, arguing that the case still being under investigation before the Burundian courts, the Commission's decision to declare the Communication admissible was in contradiction with the provisions of Article 56(5) on the exhaustion of local remedies.

To justify the undue prolongation of local remedies, the Respondent State submitted that this was due to the fact that the victim's family had never responded to the summonses addressed to it, which would have slowed down the procedure.
However as in its previous submission, the State has provided no proof of the existence of the summonses which it claims to have sent to the victim's family and which allegedly remained unanswered.

In accordance with the provisions of Rule 103 of the Rules of Procedure on preliminary objections, the Secretariat transmitted the State's objection to the Complainants so that they could submit a written response to the State's arguments.
In response to the State's request, the Complainants emphasised that it brought no new element capable of justifying the review of the decision on the admissibility of the Communication.

Indeed, concerning the prolongation of the investigation files allegedly opened, the Complainants submit that the State is attempting to argue that the facts denounced in the Communication in question still fall within the jurisdiction of the Burundian courts by invoking the opening and investigation of the file on the attempted assassination, while imputing the recorded prolongation to the victim's family which allegedly did not respond to the summonses of the Court. However, the State provides no proof showing the existence of these summonses which the victim's family has always affirmed never to have received. It is therefore legitimate to call into question the veracity of its assertions.

They further add that in the event that these "multiple" summonses had actually been sent to the family of the late Mr Audace Vianney, but that the latter refused to appear, this lack of response would not suffice to justify the prolongation of the investigations, notably when the various prerogatives available to the Public Prosecutor's Office as the supreme prosecuting authority are recalled. Indeed, in light of Law No. 1/10 of 3 April 2013 revising the Code of Criminal Procedure and applicable at the time of the facts, the Public Prosecutor's Office has the possibility of resorting to a list of diligent actions to ensure that the persons summoned appear. Indeed, in light of articles 79, 82, 83, 335 and 336 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Public Prosecutor's Office has the possibility of issuing warrants to bring and summonses to appear, and also has the possibility of referring an individual before the competent judge.
The Complainants emphasise that the State has made use of none of the numerous prerogatives at its disposal.

For the Complainants, the State's postulate in maintaining that the existence of a judicial file on the first attempted assassination suffices to keep the case under Burundian jurisdiction, while omitting to provide elements concerning the judicial investigation file opened under number RMP 137164/ NR/BB relating to the extrajudicial execution of July 2011, hardly pleads in its favour. Indeed, the State passes over in silence the very existence of this investigation file, and does not provide material proof of the various diligent actions that it was required to use to find the alleged perpetrators of the extrajudicial execution of Mr Audace Vianney.

The Complainants consider that in view of the nature of the violations alleged in this case, and in the face of the State's lack of justification to explain why nearly nine (9) years after the discovery of the victim's body, the file is still under investigation, and in view of the absence of elements showing any diligence on its part in prosecuting the facts, it should be found that the delays in the present case have been unduly prolonged.

The Complainants also submit that contrary to what is put forward by the Respondent State the non-existence of a legal and institutional framework for the protection of victims and witnesses of human rights violations had been initially emphasised by the authors to argue that it was dangerous for the family of the late Mr Audace Vianney to pursue further steps at the national level and to request the granting of provisional measures, and not to argue about the normal or abnormal prolongation of the investigations at the domestic level.

Moreover, it should be noted that at the time of filing the initial Communication, namely in 2014, the authors had emphasised the absence of a legal and institutional framework for the protection of victims and witnesses of human rights violations, this having moreover been the argument presented to request provisional measures for the benefit of the victim's family. They add that even if the protection framework was established by the adoption of Law No. 1/04 of 27 June 2016, cited by the Respondent State. However, in view of the persistence of violations and impunity in Burundi, it is clear that the adoption of this new legal framework has had no tangible impact on the situation of victims and on their protection.

Then, in its 2017 report, the Commission of Inquiry on Burundi indicated that it had "collected testimonies from refugees who have received anonymous threats by telephone or written messages, and who have even been physically attacked" and that "allegations of reprisals and threats against Burundians who have collaborated in the past with international human rights mechanisms, or who have testified to representatives of the United Nations, NGOs or journalists, have led the Commission to pay particular attention to the protection of victims, witnesses and all other sources".

The Commission of Inquiry also reiterated the vulnerability of victims in Burundi in its report of 12 September 2018, in which it emphasised that many victims did not lodge complaints notably because they were "afraid of the possible consequences if they lodged a complaint". It also noted "numerous cases of threats and reprisals to discourage victims or their families from lodging complaints have been reported to the Commission" and it was also emphasised that "[t]he absence of an official procedure for the protection of witnesses and victims despite the adoption of a law to that effect exacerbates the risks for victims".
In view of the arguments set out, the Complainants consider that the Commission should not act on the State's request and should proceed to the examination of the merits of the present communication.

Rule 103 of the Rules of Procedure of the African Commission, provides the conditions allowing either party to raise a preliminary objection at the admissibility stage or before the Commission takes a decision on the merits of the Communication.

According to the provisions of Rule 103 (1) this must be done no later than thirty (30) days after receipt of notification to submit a brief on admissibility or on the merits. Paragraph 4 of the said Rule provides that when the Commission receives a preliminary objection, it must first examine it before any other question relating to the Communication.

On analysis of the arguments presented by the Respondent State, with a view to contesting the decision on admissibility, it appears that the State is principally relying on the existence of an investigation under way before its courts.

The State also submits that the undue prolongation of local remedies is justified by the fact that the members of the victim's family never responded to the summonses addressed to them, which would have slowed down the procedure. Thus for the State by declaring the Communication admissible the Commission violates the provisions of Article 56(5) on the exhaustion of local remedies.

In response to the State's arguments, the Complainants argue that no new element has been brought by the State which merely asserts without providing any proof capable of supporting its arguments. The Complainants also request that the Commission maintain its decision and proceed to the examination of the Communication on the merits.

Rule 104(3) of the Rules of Procedure on the review of a decision of inadmissibility of a Communication stipulates that to be reconsidered, new elements must be submitted to the attention of the Commission by the Complainants.
In the present case it is a question of reviewing the decision on admissibility rendered by the Commission after a legal analysis of the facts and arguments before it.

The Commission notes that the State's arguments are similar to the previous arguments that it had put forward during the examination of admissibility and on the basis of which the Commission had declared the Communication in question admissible. following the inability of the State to provide the necessary evidence aimed at supporting the inadmissibility of the Communication.

Indeed, the Commission recalls that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies listed in Article 56(5) of the African Charter cannot apply if the remedies in question are not available, effective or satisfactory. The Commission has also established the fact that if the complainant cannot go before a court in his or her country because he or she fears for his or her life or for that of members of his or her family, the remedies are considered non-existent.

Moreover, in its Communication 426/12 – Agnès Uwimana-Nkusi & Saidati Mukakibibi (represented by Media Legal Defence Initiative) v. Rwanda, the Commission had held that in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity and Article 56(5) of the Charter which requires the exhaustion of local remedies as a precondition for the filing of communications, it does not serve as an appeal body for national courts, and that "in assessing the compatibility of the decision of a national court with the African Charter, the African Commission does not act as an appellate body with the power to overturn the decisions of national courts, but simply performs its mandate of ensuring compliance by a State party with the provisions of the African Charter in its interpretation and application of the law." In the present case it is by no means a question of examining the conformity of the decision of a national court with the African Charter, but of the non-existence of a decision at the national level due to the prolonged length of the judicial proceedings. Consequently, the decision on admissibility taken by the Commission is in conformity with its mandate.

Although the State has attempted to provide arguments concerning the undue prolongation of local remedies, it has provided no information concerning the effectiveness and satisfactoriness of these remedies which are also contested by the Complainants. Moreover, as in its previous submissions the arguments put forward are not supported by any concrete proof and may therefore be considered as mere unfounded assertions.

The analysis of the State's request having highlighted no new element in relation to the arguments submitted during the examination of admissibility and the arguments put forward being the same as those that had already been the subject of an analysis concluding that the Communication was admissible, the Commission decides to maintain its decision on the admissibility of the Communication and to proceed to its analysis on the merits.

The Complainants allege the violation of the following articles of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter): 2, 4, 5, read together with Article 1 as well as 6, 7 (1) (a), 18 (1) and 26.

The provisions of Article 2 of the African Charter, entitle every individual to the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognised and guaranteed in the Charter without distinction of any kind, notably [...] political or any other opinion".

The Complainants submit that the Commission has considered this provision as constituting a fundamental aspect of human rights given that its existence or absence affects the ability of everyone to enjoy other rights. In other words, it makes it the foundation of the enjoyment of all human rights.

They also add that the Commission has indicated that "discrimination can be defined as the application of any distinction, exclusion, restriction or preference based on grounds such as [political opinion] which has the purpose or effect of nullifying or impairing the recognition, enjoyment or exercise by all persons, on an equal footing, of all rights and freedoms.

The Complainants further emphasise the obligation of States parties "to ensure by appropriate means that persons placed under their jurisdiction are not discriminated against on any of the grounds prohibited by the treaty to which they have subscribed "in accordance with Article 1 of the African Charter".

They report that former FNL members, of whom the victim was one, were particularly targeted by serious human rights violations during the post-electoral period. They suffered restrictions on their rights because of their commitment to an opposition party. They were hunted down by the intelligence services who asked them to reveal the names of the FNL leaders. Consequently a large number of members and former members of the FNL went into hiding after having received threats.

Moreover, more than 130 extrajudicial executions have taken place in Burundi since 2010 and the great majority of the victims are Hutu activists or former fighters who belonged to the FNL, according to the reports established by the United Nations Office present on the ground.

Mr Audace Vianney, having been clearly identified as a former FNL member, the Complainants consider that the latter was the victim of discrimination based on his political opinion, which resulted in serious violations of his rights and led to his extrajudicial execution.
The Complainants request the Commission to find a violation of Article 2 of the African Charter against Mr Audace Vianney by the Burundian State.

The Complainants submit that the provisions of Article 4 of the African Charter which guarantees to every human being the right to respect for his life and the integrity of his person have been violated by the Respondent State which failed in its duty to protect human life against gratuitous or arbitrary actions of public authorities and private persons.

For the Complainants, two main elements emerge from the jurisprudence of the African Commission which make it possible to characterise a violation of the right to life as an extrajudicial execution. First, the execution must have been committed by an agent of the State or with its consent. In addition, the execution must follow an arbitrary - inappropriate, unfair, unpredictable or unlawful - trial or not be preceded by any consent.

They maintain that the African Commission has recognised that extrajudicial executions constitute a violation of the right to life protected under Article 4 of the African Charter. Consequently, they consider that when a violation of the right to life has been caused by an agent of the State following an arbitrary trial or outside any judicial procedure, it is an extrajudicial execution, whatever the motivations and intentions of those responsible or the conditions surrounding the violation.
They also add that the Commission has already characterised as extrajudicial execution deprivations of the right to life committed by State agents outside the framework of trials.

They emphasise the obligation of States to investigate effectively and diligently violations of the right to life, as well as their responsibility to protect all persons under their jurisdiction against non-State actors, notably the duty to take preventive operational measures to protect a person whose life is in danger from the criminal acts of another person.

The Complainants finally submit that in the present case, it should be emphasised that Mr Audace Vianney was the subject of an attempted assassination on 7 March 2011, while he was at his home. Moreover, it is established that agents of the Burundian State were involved in this attempted violation of the right to life, notably Mr Cyrille Nahimana, whose responsibility for attempted assassination was recognised by the Prosecutor who covered a judicial procedure against him. Consequently, the attempted violation of the right to life caused by State agents outside the framework of a trial, must be found to have been an attempted extrajudicial execution against the victim. This attempt would moreover become an absolute violation of his right to life, when he was found dead on 15 July 2011, with several bullets in his body.
In view of the foregoing the Commission is therefore requested to find a violation of Article 4 by the State of Burundi.

Under the terms of Article 5 of the African Charter [e]very individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited.

The Complainants submit that Mr Audace Vianney was the victim of torture, of cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment as well as of serious violation of his right to dignity and legal personality as enshrined in Article 5 of the African Charter.

They affirm that the African Commission considers the right to human dignity as "a fundamental right which all human beings must enjoy without any discrimination, irrespective of their mental capacities or incapacities, as the case may be. It is consequently a natural right which every human being is obliged to respect, by all means, and which also confers on every human being the duty to respect it".

They add that the Commission has adopted a broad interpretation of the notion of dignity, considering that Article 5 of the Charter protects not only the physical person of the victim but also the minimum economic and social circumstances required for human existence. They add that it is generally accepted that legal personality has a natural origin and derives from the very essence of the being to which it is attached. Thus the right to legal personality embodies the notions of human dignity and integrity of the person, entailing a right to legality. It is a right to have rights whose respect is a necessary precondition for the realisation of all individual rights.

Thus, serious violations of the life and integrity of a person who is removed from the protection of the law constitute violations of dignity and legal personality, which is the case of Mr Audace Vianney.

Indeed, the Complainants maintain that the victim was removed from the protection of the law, after having been the subject of an attempted assassination on 7 March 2011 at his home by State agents. He was also the target of several acts of harassment and intimidation by State representatives right up to his death preceded by a disappearance on 14 July until the discovery of his body riddled with bullets on 15 July 2011.

They further consider that Mr Audace Vianney as well as his family were victims of torture, the former following the attempted assassination of which he was a victim when three bullets were fired at him leaving him in a coma for nearly three months and then through the various acts of intimidation and harassment to which he was subjected and which may constitute acts of psychological torture. The latter (his family) through the anxiety and anguish caused by the treatment inflicted on the victim, but also by the uncertainty for its future caused by the death of Mr Audace Vianney. In support of their arguments, they submit that the Human Rights Committee has consistently recognised in its jurisprudence that "the anguish and distress that the disappearance [...] has caused to all his close family" constitutes a violation of Article 7 of the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights with regard to the relatives of the victim.

The Complainants also maintain that the State failed in its obligation of protection by not having taken the necessary measures to prevent the occurrence of acts of torture against Mr Audace Vianney and his family, as well as by not putting in place "effective remedies in a transparent, independent and effective legal system" and by not pursuing effective and independent investigations relating to these allegations.
The Complainants request to be heard on this ground by the Commission and that it find a violation of Article 5 of the African Charter.

Article 6 of the African Charter provides that every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law.

The Complainants recall that in its jurisprudence, the African Commission analyses Article 6 on two distinct and complementary aspects; the right to liberty and the right to security of the person. The right to liberty benefits every individual and constitutes a fundamental condition for the enjoyment of other rights and "to be deprived of it is a fact which seems to have a direct and undesirable effect on the enjoyment of several other rights, ranging from the right to a family and a private life, through freedom of assembly, association and expression, to the right to freedom of movement".

It therefore presupposes the right to be free from any constraint, subject to respect for the law. In this respect Article 6 of the African Charter protects individuals against arbitrary arrests and detentions. It therefore implies that Article 6 must be interpreted in such a way as to permit arrests only in the exercise of the powers normally vested in law enforcement forces in a democratic society.

As regards the right to security, the Complainants submit that the African Commission has considered that it is "an expression of rights based on the prohibition of torture and of cruel and unusual punishment" even though, more often, the right to security protects the person against conduct less damaging to physical and psychological integrity. Thus in the public sphere this right refers to the obligation of the State to protect "the physical integrity of its citizens against abuses committed by public authorities".
The Complainants therefore consider that the State failed in its obligation of protection towards Mr Audace Vianney against abuses by public authorities.

In support of their assertion, they recall the circumstances preceding the death of Mr Audace Vianney, notably the acts of harassment and intimidation by duly identified representatives of the public authority, the attempted assassination at his home through to his abduction which led to his extrajudicial execution.

They also recall that several positive obligations flow from the right to liberty and security of person and that by virtue of Article 6, the State must protect individuals from infringements of their liberty and security and must also prevent such violations and investigate them when they occur in order to prosecute and punish the perpetrators and grant full reparation to the victims.
Consequently, they request the Commission to find a violation of Article 6 by the Respondent State.

Article 7(1) (a) of the African Charter provides that "[e]very individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: [...] the right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force."

The Complainants submit that the African Commission has interpreted this article as recognising for complainants the right to have "unimpeded access to a court or competent jurisdiction to hear their case"

They also affirm that the rights protected under Article 7(1) (a) are recognised for persons arrested and detained but also for any other individual, and that the African Commission has considered that when victims are prevented from accessing the courts to have their case heard, State authorities violate Article 7 (1) (a) of the African Charter and likewise "when the competent authorities put obstacles in the way of victims' access to the courts, they must be held responsible"

They further add that the obstacles which may prevent victims' access to the courts have been identified by the jurisprudence of the African Commission which has considered among other things that situations or acts of violence committed against victims may render access to the competent bodies to obtain justice illusory and impossible and thus constitute a violation of Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter.

Article 26 of the African Charter imposes on States "the duty to guarantee the independence of the Courts", an essential component for guaranteeing victims an effective remedy before domestic judicial institutions.
The Complainants submit that the African Commission has already found a violation of Article 26 in connection with Article 7(1)(a), when the impartiality of the courts was not guaranteed.

In the present case, although a judicial file was indeed opened following the attempted assassination of March 2011 against the person of Mr Audace Vianney and Mr Cyrille Nahimana was charged, no prosecution was initiated against him, leaving him free to continue these acts of intimidation towards the victim. Then, no investigation was conducted concerning the extrajudicial execution of which Mr Audace Vianney was a victim, despite the heavy media coverage of this event and the existence of a judicial file concerning an attempted assassination against him.

The Complainants consider that the lack of action by Burundian justice stems from the "general climate of impunity", prevailing in Burundi with regard to serious human rights violations. They also cite the report of the Commission of Inquiry on extrajudicial executions and acts of torture set up in June 2011 which although having recognised the commission of homicide denied the fact that these were extrajudicial executions.

Moreover, the question of the independence of the judiciary in Burundi has been raised on several occasions including during the Burundian Estates General of Justice held from 5 to 9 August 2013 which highlighted the need to reform the system to ensure its independence, notably by formulating recommendations concerning the independence of the judiciary vis-à-vis the executive, a subject of central concern during the discussions. Indeed, among the main conclusions were the reform of the Higher Council of the Judiciary whose presidency is vested in the President of the Republic and the election of the President of the Supreme Court who is appointed by the President instead of being elected. The Complainants consider that the conclusions of the Estates General of Justice found a lack of independence vis-à-vis the executive.

Finally, the Complainants maintain that the State agents alleged to be responsible in this case are the perpetrators of numerous serious human rights violations and particularly benefit from this generalised impunity.

In view of the absence of results of the proceedings opened and of the more general contextual elements presented above, the Complainants respectfully request the Commission to find a violation of Articles 7(1) (a) and 26 of the African Charter against the rightful claimants of Mr Audace Vianney.

Article 18(1) of the African Charter provides that "[t]he family shall be the natural unit and basis of society. It shall be protected by the State which shall take care of its physical health and moral".

The Complainants submit that the African Commission has considered that the separation of members of a family resulting from arbitrary and incommunicado detention constitutes a violation of the right to family life and thus of Article 18(1) of the African Charter.

They also submit that the jurisprudence of the United Nations Human Rights Committee has specified the scope of the right to protection of the family provided for in Article 23 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Concluding notably in the case Marcel Mulezi v. Democratic Republic of the Congo, that the death of the author's wife as a result of ill-treatment inflicted by State agents constituted a violation of this provision.

Likewise the execution of Mr Audace Vianney entailed a breakdown of family unity and an impairment of the psychological health of the members of the family. Indeed, the death of the victim had a negative impact on his wife and his mother who fell into emotional distress affecting their health, but also deprived a young child of his father. Furthermore the death of Mr Audace Vianney also put his family in a situation of economic precariousness because he was the one who provided for its needs.
Consequently the Complainants respectfully request the Commission to find a violation of Article 18(1) of the African Charter against the relatives of Mr Audace Vianney Habonarugira.

As the procedure indicates, despite the time far beyond the deadlines prescribed by the Commission's Rules of Procedure and the reminder addressed to it, the Respondent State has not transmitted its observations on the merits.

Article 2 of the African Charter guarantees to every individual the enjoyment of the rights and freedoms recognised and guaranteed in the Charter without distinction of any kind such as race, ethnic group, colour, sex, language, religion, political or any other opinion, national and social origin, fortune, birth or other status.

The Complainants maintain that the victim was clearly identified as a former member of the FNL, the former members of the FNL, were particularly targeted by serious human rights violations during the post-electoral period of 2010. They suffered restrictions on their rights because of their commitment to an opposition party. They were hunted down by the intelligence services who asked them to reveal the names of the FNL leaders. Consequently a large number of members and former members of the FNL went into hiding after having received threats.
